title: The garden owners
hook: owners of a garden plan to harvest before the poor come, and find it burned (68:17–33)

segments.voice: Yesterday: khuluq, and your line, great character. Did the trait you picked get tested? Today al-Qalam tells a story, about some people whose character failed one morning. Day six hundred forty-two.

It's the night before harvest. A garden full of fruit, heavy on the branches. The owners, brothers in the commentators' retelling, sit together and make a plan. Tomorrow, early, before anyone's awake, we go out and pick it all. Quietly. And they swear to it. No poor person gets through the gate today. They go to bed pleased with themselves. They don't know that something is already moving through their garden in the dark.

Surah al-Qalam, verses seventeen to thirty-three. The owners swore they'd harvest in the morning, and the Qur'an adds a small detail: they made no exception. Commentators understand that as: they didn't say in sha' Allah, if God wills. They spoke as if tomorrow was theirs. Then, while they slept, a visitation from their Lord passed over the garden, and by morning it was like a field already reaped, black, stripped. At dawn they called to one another, set out, whispering on the road: let no needy person come in on you today. They arrived, and at first they didn't recognize it. We must have lost our way, they said. Then: no, we've been deprived. Then the turn. The middlemost of them, the most balanced one, says: didn't I tell you? Why didn't you glorify Allah? And they did. They said glory to our Lord, we were wrong. Then they turned on each other, blaming. Then they admitted it together: we were the ones who overstepped. And they ended with hope: perhaps our Lord will give us something better in its place. The Qur'an doesn't tell us where this garden was or who the men were. Commentators tell a fuller story: the garden belonged to a good man in Yemen who always left a share for the poor, and after he died his sons decided to stop. That backstory comes from the commentaries, not the verses. But the verses are clear enough. They lost the whole harvest trying to keep the poor's share. And the story doesn't end in the ashes. It ends in repentance and hope.

The practice: share part of something before you use it. Sit, and think of something you'll receive or use today: a paycheck, a meal, a bag of groceries, a free hour. Picture it in your hands. Now picture setting aside a small part before you start, not from the leftovers, from the top. A coin, a plate for a neighbor, ten minutes for someone who needs it. Decide what that share is. The bell holds the time.
No exception. In 68:17–33 the garden owners swore to harvest by morning without saying if God wills, lost everything overnight, and returned in repentance. Today's word.
Your line: the poor's share first. Today, before you spend or eat or use something, set a small part aside for someone else, from the top. Day six hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims give zakat on harvests and wealth and voluntary charity (sadaqah); saying in sha' Allah, if God wills, of future plans follows 18:23–24, and the story of the garden owners is told to teach both.

original.note: Arabic, 68:18: and they made no exception, understood as not saying in sha' Allah.

trapdoor: what you thought: greedy people get punished.
what it means: they planned to cut out the poor and spoke as if tomorrow was theirs, then lost it all, and turned back.

sources.ref: classical tafsir on 68:17–33 (the father who gave to the poor; the garden in Yemen)
Qur'an 18:23–24 (say 'if Allah wills' of future plans)

notes: The whole story is paraphrased from 68:17–33; confirm the sequence: oath, 'no exception', visitation by night, whispering, 'we have lost our way' / 'we are deprived', the middlemost one, blaming, admission, hope.
'Brothers in many retellings' and the Yemen/father backstory come from tafsir; both are marked as such in the script.
Reading la yastathnun as not saying in sha' Allah is the majority interpretation; confirm.
'Like a field already reaped, black' paraphrases as-sarim; commentators differ (reaped, or dark as night).

The hook and index say the garden was found 'burned'; the verses say only that a visitation passed over it and it became as-sarim. Burning (a fire) is a tafsir reading. The script body avoids it; a Keeper may want the hook to say 'ruined' instead (left unchanged here because the hook mirrors the curriculum index).
